steps.title: Data & leakage control
steps.label: Data
steps.what: Used the public Lending Club loan book (2007-2018) and kept only resolved loans, labelling Charged Off and Default as default. Dropped every post-origination variable (recoveries, payments, last payment dates) and the lender's own grade and interest rate from the main feature set.
steps.why: Those variables are consequences of the outcome or copies of the lender's own model, so using them would make the prediction circular.
steps.learned: The lender's own grade still beats the leakage-free model by about {auc_gap} AUC. I report it as an upper bound, not as a flaw.

steps.title: An honest validation split
steps.label: Validation
steps.what: Found that recent loans are right-censored (still open), derived the split from the data with a rule of at least 90% resolved, and trained on 2010-2013 and tested on 2014-2015 with 36-month loans. Every fitted element (winsorization, encoders, WoE) uses training data only.
steps.why: A random split leaks the credit cycle, and censored vintages mix real signal with a measurement artifact.
steps.learned: The censored 2017-2018 window flatters the model (AUC {window_immature_auc} vs {champion_auc}), so it is shown only to measure that gap.

steps.title: Scorecard and challengers
steps.label: Scorecard
steps.what: Binned variables with WoE and ranked them by IV; screened correlation and VIF, leaving 7 predictors for a logit scorecard (base score 600, odds 1:50, 20 points to double the odds). Compared it with Lasso, Ridge, a tree, a random forest and LightGBM tuned by temporal cross-validation, and explained the champion with SHAP.
steps.why: The scorecard is interpretable; the challengers show how much more a flexible model captures from the full 30-variable set.
steps.learned: LightGBM wins (AUC {champion_auc} vs {scorecard_auc} for the scorecard), but discrimination remains moderate.

steps.title: Calibration and LGD
steps.label: Calibration
steps.what: Compared four probability calibrators (none, intercept, Platt, isotonic) fitted on a later out-of-sample slice, and modelled LGD with a Gamma GLM, LightGBM and a two-part model for the mass at LGD = 1.
steps.why: A calibrator fitted in-sample inherits the overfit it should fix, and realised LGD piles up at 0 and 1.
steps.learned: Calibration did not improve the Brier score and no LGD model had a positive out-of-time R-squared, so expected loss uses the portfolio-level LGD ({realized_lgd}). Both are reported as null results.

steps.title: Portfolio loss simulation
steps.label: Simulation
steps.what: Built a Vasicek single-factor Monte Carlo over grade x PD-decile buckets, swept asset correlation from 0.02 to 0.15 (including the Basel-implied {rho_basel}), added PD and LGD stress, and tested stratified, antithetic and importance-sampling variance reduction.
steps.why: Correlation is a portfolio effect, so averaging PD first would hide the tail.
steps.learned: Importance sampling cuts the tail-VaR error by {is_rmse_factor} times, while antithetic sampling gives almost nothing. Capital figures depend strongly on the correlation.
